They stay out of it. I’m going to stay out of Connecticut. You were born there. That general dynamic is why it’s so strange. Pretend that I’m on the ballot. I’m on the ballot. I’m on. Instead, what this convention does is bind Republicans and Trump even closer. This is the Republican Convention. It tells voters that if you cast a ballot for a Republican politician, you’re casting a ballot for Trump. It feels like profound political malpractice, given the extent to which Republicans will need to distance themselves from Trump in order to make any ground, any headway. Perhaps that’s the reason that so many vulnerable candidates, candidates in swing states and swing districts, did not show up. Really, the story has become who’s not attending. They are aware of the danger this poses to their odds. The gambit here appears to be that if you can create this tight connection between Trump and Republican candidates, then you can bring out some of the infrequent voters who turned out for Trump in 2024. You know what happens if you don’t vote? You go to hell. But sometimes the political conventional wisdom is conventional wisdom for a reason. There’s a reason that the midterm convention is not a thing. Everybody said, if you have a midterm convention, it’s going to be a disaster. And that is because in a midterm year, the odds that you’re able to generate enough enthusiasm to offset the structural disadvantages and the president’s unpopularity are extremely low. Infrequent voters are infrequent for a reason. They haven’t made a habit of voting. They don’t turn out on the regular. And it takes a lot of energy. It takes a lot of resources to turn them out. Perhaps this will work. Perhaps urging identification with Trump will work. Perhaps making this promise of a $5,000 payment will work. I don’t know the practicality of it, but sure, why not. The funny thing about all of this really is when it probably doesn’t work in November, when it probably falls flat, Donald Trump isn’t going to take any responsibility. He’s going to blame Republicans. Maybe it will work out, and it will help Republicans hold on to one or both chambers of Congress. And I don’t take it because it’s just not authentic. It’s not genuine. Right. I also do feel as if, like, all money is not good money. Yeah. Do what you want to do. Take the money if you want to. North Division for the 2026 N.F.L. season.","transcript":"Who’s going to win the N.F.C. North in 2026? Right now, it looks like the most competitive division in the N.F.L. The reigning champions, the Chicago Bears, are coming off a backbreaking Divisional Round loss to the Rams. They added linebacker Devin Bush, and shipped wide receiver DJ Moore to the Bills to make more room for Luther Burden in that offense. Can Ben Johnson and Co. recreate that worst-to-first magic that propelled them so far a year ago? Johnson’s old team, the Detroit Lions, missed the playoffs entirely last season. It’s fair to wonder, is the Super Bowl window for Dan Campbell closed? If anybody’s going to propel that team back to the top of the division, its dynamic running back Jahmyr Gibbs. Armed with a lucrative new contract extension, and a backfield all to himself without David Montgomery in the fold. In Minnesota, can supposed quarterback guru Kevin O’Connell help revive the career of Kyler Murray? And now that Brian Flores is the highest-paid defensive coordinator in the N.F.L., can that defense help propel the Vikings back into contention? In Green Bay, Jordan Love might have to put the team on his back for the first part of the season. When is Micah Parsons going to return? Can MarShawn Lloyd step up without Josh Jacobs? Are Tucker Kraft, Devonte Wyatt and Zach Bako-Bewele going to return to form off significant injuries? If all those questions pan out, the Packers probably have the most talented roster in the division. That corner of policy that is being influenced by the president’s making of money off of foreign entities, giving his entities money, does count as kleptocracy. So this is a harder question than you might think. Not obviously yet. The president is not subject to the conflict of interest regime that the rest of the federal government, except for the vice president, is subject to. One remedy for conflict of interest is recusal. The president can’t recuse. He’s in charge of everything. So in the last 50, 60, 70 years, we developed alternate strategies to deal with conflicts. Norms that every president until Trump with tiny little deviations followed. So there’s not a whole lot of law governing it. There’s the bribery laws, which are very hard to meet. Then came an unprecedented punishment from the league.","transcript":"Take me back to the moment you learned about the unprecedented sentence that the N.B.A. was handing down. When I see confirmation of that, one part of me, of course, just takes an enormous exhale. People saying you’ve been a liar and a fraud and a clout- chaser this whole time, blah, blah, blah, blah, blah, all that stuff. And I’m online. I’m on the internet, you know, I saw and felt this stuff. It sucked. I never, though, wavered in our reporting. And so for me, it has been, yes, vindicating on some level, but really encouraging. And I say encouraging because we’re living in an era in which there just aren’t consequences for people this wealthy when stuff like this happens in general. They stay out of it. I’m going to stay out of Connecticut. You were born there. That general dynamic is why it’s so strange. Pretend that I’m on the ballot. I’m on the ballot. I’m on. Instead, what this convention does is bind Republicans and Trump even closer. This is the Republican Convention. It tells voters that if you cast a ballot for a Republican politician, you’re casting a ballot for Trump. It feels like profound political malpractice, given the extent to which Republicans will need to distance themselves from Trump in order to make any ground, any headway. Perhaps that’s the reason that so many vulnerable candidates, candidates in swing states and swing districts, did not show up. Really, the story has become who’s not attending. They are aware of the danger this poses to their odds. The gambit here appears to be that if you can create this tight connection between Trump and Republican candidates, then you can bring out some of the infrequent voters who turned out for Trump in 2024. You know what happens if you don’t vote? You go to hell. But sometimes the political conventional wisdom is conventional wisdom for a reason. There’s a reason that the midterm convention is not a thing. Everybody said, if you have a midterm convention, it’s going to be a disaster. And that is because in a midterm year, the odds that you’re able to generate enough enthusiasm to offset the structural disadvantages and the president’s unpopularity are extremely low. Infrequent voters are infrequent for a reason. They haven’t made a habit of voting. They don’t turn out on the regular. And it takes a lot of energy. It takes a lot of resources to turn them out. Perhaps this will work. Perhaps urging identification with Trump will work. Perhaps making this promise of a $5,000 payment will work. I don’t know the practicality of it, but sure, why not. The funny thing about all of this really is when it probably doesn’t work in November, when it probably falls flat, Donald Trump isn’t going to take any responsibility. He’s going to blame Republicans. Maybe it will work out, and it will help Republicans hold on to one or both chambers of Congress. And I don’t take it because it’s just not authentic. It’s not genuine. Right. I also do feel as if, like, all money is not good money. Yeah. Do what you want to do. Take the money if you want to. North Division for the 2026 N.F.L. season.","transcript":"Who’s going to win the N.F.C. North in 2026? Right now, it looks like the most competitive division in the N.F.L. The reigning champions, the Chicago Bears, are coming off a backbreaking Divisional Round loss to the Rams. They added linebacker Devin Bush, and shipped wide receiver DJ Moore to the Bills to make more room for Luther Burden in that offense. Can Ben Johnson and Co. recreate that worst-to-first magic that propelled them so far a year ago? Johnson’s old team, the Detroit Lions, missed the playoffs entirely last season. It’s fair to wonder, is the Super Bowl window for Dan Campbell closed? If anybody’s going to propel that team back to the top of the division, its dynamic running back Jahmyr Gibbs. Armed with a lucrative new contract extension, and a backfield all to himself without David Montgomery in the fold. In Minnesota, can supposed quarterback guru Kevin O’Connell help revive the career of Kyler Murray? And now that Brian Flores is the highest-paid defensive coordinator in the N.F.L., can that defense help propel the Vikings back into contention? In Green Bay, Jordan Love might have to put the team on his back for the first part of the season. When is Micah Parsons going to return? Can MarShawn Lloyd step up without Josh Jacobs? Are Tucker Kraft, Devonte Wyatt and Zach Bako-Bewele going to return to form off significant injuries? If all those questions pan out, the Packers probably have the most talented roster in the division. That corner of policy that is being influenced by the president’s making of money off of foreign entities, giving his entities money, does count as kleptocracy. So this is a harder question than you might think. Not obviously yet. The president is not subject to the conflict of interest regime that the rest of the federal government, except for the vice president, is subject to. One remedy for conflict of interest is recusal. The president can’t recuse. He’s in charge of everything. So in the last 50, 60, 70 years, we developed alternate strategies to deal with conflicts. Norms that every president until Trump with tiny little deviations followed. So there’s not a whole lot of law governing it. There’s the bribery laws, which are very hard to meet. Then came an unprecedented punishment from the league.","transcript":"Take me back to the moment you learned about the unprecedented sentence that the N.B.A. was handing down. When I see confirmation of that, one part of me, of course, just takes an enormous exhale. People saying you’ve been a liar and a fraud and a clout- chaser this whole time, blah, blah, blah, blah, blah, all that stuff. And I’m online. I’m on the internet, you know, I saw and felt this stuff. It sucked. I never, though, wavered in our reporting. And so for me, it has been, yes, vindicating on some level, but really encouraging. And I say encouraging because we’re living in an era in which there just aren’t consequences for people this wealthy when stuff like this happens in general.     <script>
      const categorySlugRemoval = () => {
          const HOST = "help.nytimes.com";
          if (location.hostname !== HOST) return;
        
          const parts = location.pathname.split("/").filter(Boolean);
          if (parts.length < 2) return;
        
          let slugIndex = -1;         
          for (let i = parts.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) {
            if (/^\d+-[A-Za-z0-9-]+$/.test(parts[i])) {
              slugIndex = i;
              break;
            }
          }
          if (slugIndex <= 0) return;           
        
          const keep = parts.slice(slugIndex);       
          const cleanURL = `${location.origin}/${keep.join("/")}${location.search}${location.hash}`;
        
          if (cleanURL !== location.href) {
            location.replace(cleanURL);
          }
        }
        
        categorySlugRemoval();
    </script>
    
    <script>
        const initAnchorJump = () => {
          console.log("[AnchorJump] Initializing...");
        
          const HOSTS = [
            "help.nytimes.com",
            "thenewyorktimeshelpcenter.helpjuice.com"
          ];
        
          const SAME_PAGE = (u) => {
            const result =
              HOSTS.includes(u.hostname) &&
              HOSTS.includes(location.hostname) &&
              u.pathname.replace(/\/+$/, "") === location.pathname.replace(/\/+$/, "");
            console.log(`[AnchorJump] SAME_PAGE check for ${u.href}:`, result);
            return result;
          };
        
          const findTarget = (frag, root) => {
            console.log(`[AnchorJump] Looking for target "${frag}" inside`, root);
            const el = root.querySelector(`[id="${frag}"], [id*="${frag}"]`);
            console.log(`[AnchorJump] Target found:`, el);
            return el;
          };
        
          const jumpTo = (el) => {
            if (!el) {
              console.log("[AnchorJump] jumpTo called with null element!");
              return;
            }
            console.log(`[AnchorJump] Jumping to element with id="${el.id}"...`);
            if (el.scrollIntoView) {
              el.scrollIntoView({ block: "start", inline: "nearest" });
              console.log("[AnchorJump] Used scrollIntoView.");
            } else {
              const scroller = document.scrollingElement || document.documentElement || document.body;
              const rectTop = el.getBoundingClientRect().top;
              scroller.scrollTop = scroller.scrollTop + rectTop;
              console.log("[AnchorJump] Manually set scrollTop.");
            }
          };
        
          document.querySelectorAll(".helpjuice-article-body-content").forEach((container, idx) => {
            console.log(`[AnchorJump] Setting up listener for container #${idx}`);
            container.addEventListener("click", (e) => {
              console.log("[AnchorJump] Click detected:", e.target);
        
              const a = e.target.closest('a[href*="#"]');
              console.log("[AnchorJump] Closest anchor:", a);
              if (!a || !container.contains(a)) return;
        
              const href = a.getAttribute("href");
              console.log(`[AnchorJump] Anchor href: ${href}`);
              const u = new URL(href, location.href);
        
              if (!u.hash || !SAME_PAGE(u)) {
                console.log("[AnchorJump] Different page or no hash, skipping.");
                return;
              }
        
              let frag;
              try {
                frag = decodeURIComponent(u.hash.slice(1));
              } catch {
                frag = u.hash.slice(1);
              }
              console.log(`[AnchorJump] Fragment: "${frag}"`);
        
              const target = findTarget(frag, container) || document.getElementById(frag);
              if (!target) {
                console.log("[AnchorJump] No target found, aborting.");
                return;
              }
        
              e.preventDefault();
              jumpTo(target);
        
              if (typeof history !== "undefined" && history.pushState) {
                history.pushState(null, "", `#${encodeURIComponent(frag)}`);
                console.log(`[AnchorJump] Updated URL with pushState: #${frag}`);
              } else {
                location.hash = `#${encodeURIComponent(frag)}`;
                console.log(`[AnchorJump] Updated location.hash manually: #${frag}`);
              }
            });
          });
        
          if (location.hash) {
            console.log(`[AnchorJump] Page loaded with hash: ${location.hash}`);
            let frag;
            try {
              frag = decodeURIComponent(location.hash.slice(1));
            } catch {
              frag = location.hash.slice(1);
            }
            console.log(`[AnchorJump] Looking for target on page load: "${frag}"`);
            const target = findTarget(frag, document) || document.getElementById(frag);
            if (target) {
              jumpTo(target);
              console.log("[AnchorJump] Jumped to target on load.");
            } else {
              console.log("[AnchorJump] No target found on load.");
            }
          } else {
            console.log("[AnchorJump] No hash present on page load.");
          }
        
          console.log("[AnchorJump] Initialization complete.");
        };
        
        document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", () =>
          setTimeout(initAnchorJump, 2000)
        );

    </script>

                <div class="helpjuice-article-body-content helpjuice-editor-content"><p><span style="color:#333333;"><i>Effective on September 9, 2024</i></span></p><p>This Cookie Policy explains how we use cookies and similar tracking methods (such as pixels, SDKs, JavaScript, local storage, device identifiers, etc., which we refer to as “trackers”) when you visit our site. “Our site” means our websites, emails, apps and other services that link to this Cookie Policy, like nytimes.com and its subdomains, including The Athletic and Wirecutter.</p><p>This policy explains what various tracking methods are, and why they are used. It also explains your right to control their use.</p><p>We may change this Cookie Policy at any time. Check the “last revised” date at the top of this page to see when this Cookie Policy was last revised. Any change becomes effective when we post the revised Cookie Policy on or through our site.</p><p>Where we use trackers to collect information that is personally identifiable, or that can become personally identifiable if we combine it with other information, our Privacy Policy will apply in addition to this Cookie Policy.</p><p>If you have any questions, please contact us by email at privacy@nytimes.com. You can also write to us: The New York Times Company, 620 Eighth Avenue, New York, N.Y. 10018, attn.: Legal Department. If you have any questions regarding The Athletic, please contact The Athletic at privacy@theathletic.com.</p><h2 style="clip-path:inset(50%);clip:rect(0 0 0 0);height:1px;overflow:hidden;position:absolute;white-space:nowrap;width:1px;" id="table-of-conten-0" data-toc="false">Table of Conten</h2><h2 id="1-what-is-a-tracker-1" data-toc="true"><strong>1. What Is a Tracker? </strong></h2><p>We use a variety of tracker methods; six of the main types are explained below. This list is intended to include all categories that we use, although the categories may vary depending on the use of our site.</p><p>We use trackers to enable our servers to recognize your web browser and tell us how and when you visit and otherwise use the services through the internet, to analyze trends, and to learn about our user base so that we can improve our services and your experience.</p><p>We may combine non-personally identifiable information collected through trackers with other personal information that we have about you, for example, to tell us who you are or whether you have an account. We may also supplement the information we collect from you with information received from third parties in order to enhance our services, or to offer you information that we believe may be of interest to you.</p><p>Please reference the descriptions below to learn more about the kinds of trackers we use and for what purpose.</p><p><strong>A) Cookies</strong></p><p>A cookie is a small string of text that a website (or online service) stores on a user’s browser. It saves data on your browser about your visit to our site or other sites. It often includes a unique identifier (e.g., cookie #123).</p><p>“First-party cookies” are cookies set by us (or on our behalf) on our site. “Third-party cookies” are cookies set by other companies whose functionality is embedded into our site (e.g., google.com).</p><p>“Session cookies” are temporary cookies stored on your device while you visit our site. They expire when you close your browser. “Persistent cookies” are stored on your browser for a period of time after you leave our site. Persistent cookies expire on a set expiration date, or when they are deleted manually.</p><p>We use persistent cookies to store your preferences so that they are available for the next visit. This allows us, for example, to keep a more accurate account of how often you visit our services, how often you return, how your use of the services may vary over time, to target advertising, and measure the effectiveness of advertising efforts. Just like any other usage information we collect, this information allows us to improve the services and customize your online experience.</p><p>You can choose whether to accept cookies by editing your browser settings. However, if cookies are refused, your experience on our site may be worse, and some features may not work as intended.</p><p><strong>B) Pixels</strong></p><p>Pixels (also known as “web beacons,” “GIFs” or “bugs”) are one-pixel transparent images located on web pages or messages. They track whether you have opened these web pages or messages. Upon firing, a pixel logs a visit to the current page or message and may read or set cookies.</p><p>Pixels often rely on cookies to work, so turning off cookies can impair them. But even if you turn off cookies, pixels can still detect a web page visit.</p><p><strong>C) Javascript</strong></p><p>JavaScript is a programming language. It can be used to write trackers that, when embedded into a page, allow us to measure how you interact with our site and other sites.</p><p><strong>D) Software Development Kits (or SDKs)</strong></p><p>SDKs are pieces of code provided by our digital vendors (e.g., third-party advertising companies, ad networks and analytics providers) in our mobile apps to collect and analyze certain device and user data.</p><p><strong>E) Device Identifiers</strong></p><p>Device identifiers are user-resettable identifiers comprised of numbers and letters. They are unique to a specific device. They are stored directly on the device. They are used to recognize you and/or your devices(s) on, off and across different apps and devices for marketing and advertising purposes.</p><p><strong>F) ID Synching</strong></p><p>In order to decide what type of ad might interest you, our digital and marketing vendors sometimes link data — inferred from your browsing of other sites or collected from other sources — using a method knowns as “ID synching” or “cookie synching.” To do this, they match the tracker ID they have assigned to you with one or more tracker IDs that are held in another company’s database and that are likely also associated with you. Any of the linked trackers may have certain interests and other demographic information attributed to it. That information is then used to determine which ad to show you.</p><h2 id="2-what-trackers-do-we-use-and-for-which-purpose-2" data-toc="true"><strong>2. What Trackers Do We Use And For Which Purpose? </strong></h2><p>Below is a list of the types of trackers that appear on our site.</p><p><strong>Essential Trackers</strong></p><p>Essential trackers are required for our site to operate and to provide you with the features or services that you have requested. They allow you to navigate our site and use its services and features (e.g., cookies that help you stay logged in). Without essential trackers, our site will not run smoothly; in fact, our site (or certain services or features) might not even be available to you simply because of technical limitations.</p><p><strong>Analytics Trackers</strong></p><p>Analytics trackers collect or use information about your site use, which helps us improve our site. Among the uses of analytics trackers are to show us which pages are most frequently visited, help us record difficulties you have with our site, track subscription purchases and behaviors leading to subscription purchases, and measure how well ads perform.</p><p>These trackers add up our readers’ visits to show us larger patterns in our audience. We look at these larger patterns to analyze site traffic.</p><p><strong>Marketing Trackers</strong></p><p>These trackers help us determine which ads to show you for Times properties — both on our site and on other sites. To do this, these trackers use information about your behavior on various sites to target our ads.</p><p>These trackers allow us to limit the number of times you see our ad across your devices. They help us personalize the ads we show you. They also enable us to measure the effectiveness of our marketing campaigns (e.g., measure if you subscribe after seeing our ads).</p><p><strong>Advertising Trackers</strong></p><p>Advertising trackers help us and our advertising partners to determine which ads from third parties are selected for you. Some of these trackers collect or use information about your behavior and browsing habits on our services and other sites (including the pages you have visited, and the links and advertisements you have clicked). They also collect your demographic details, interests and certain technical information about your browser or device to aid this targeting. These trackers sometimes limit the number of times you see an ad, make an ad more relevant to you or measure the effectiveness of an ad campaign. We may not have control or access to such trackers. If you look at one page on our services, an advertisement may be delivered to you on our services or on other sites, for products referenced on that page or for similar products and services.</p><p>We work with advertisers, ad agencies and other vendors to serve these ads, who often use their own trackers through our site. The ads served can include additional trackers which are activated when an ad is visible to you or when you click on or otherwise interact with an ad.</p><h2 id="3-how-do-i-manage-trackers-3" data-toc="true"><strong>3. How Do I Manage Trackers? </strong></h2><p>In certain jurisdictions, when you first come to our site, you will receive a banner notification that trackers are present. By clicking or tapping “accept all,” you agree to the use of these trackers as described here. You can manage your tracker settings at any time by clicking on “Manage Privacy Preferences” in our website footer or in your app “Privacy Settings”, or “Account Settings” for the Athletic app.</p><p>In addition, you can refuse or accept trackers from our site (or any other site) in your browser’s settings. If you refuse trackers, you might not be able to sign in or use other tracker-dependent features of our site.</p><p>Most browsers automatically accept cookies, but this is typically something you can adjust. Information for each browser can be found in the links below:</p><p style="margin-left:1em;"><a href="https://support.apple.com/guide/safari/manage-cookies-and-website-data-sfri11471/mac"><u>Safari on desktop</u></a> and <a href="https://support.apple.com/en-us/HT201265">Safari Mobile (iPhone and iPads)</a>: Note that, by default, Safari is engineered to protect you from being tracked from site to site unless you disable Intelligent Tracking Prevention (ITP).</p><p style="margin-left:1em;"><a href="https://support.mozilla.org/en-US/kb/clear-cookies-and-site-data-firefox?redirectlocale=en-US&redirectslug=delete-cookies-remove-info-websites-stored"><u>Firefox:</u></a> By default, Firefox protects you from cross-site tracking so long as you have not disabled Total Cookie Protection. There is therefore less need to manage cookies to protect your privacy.</p><p style="margin-left:1em;"><a href="https://support.google.com/chrome/answer/95647?hl=en"><u>Chrome</u></a></p><p style="margin-left:1em;"><a href="https://support.microsoft.com/en-us/help/4468242/microsoft-edge-browsing-data-and-privacy-microsoft-privacy"><u>Microsoft Edge:</u></a> Enabling tracking prevention with Edge will protect you from being tracked between sites, such that there will be less of a need to manage your cookies in order to protect your privacy.</p><p style="margin-left:1em;"><a href="https://aboutdevice.com/clear-cookies-history-cache-on-samsung-internet-browser-android/"><u>Samsung Internet Browser:</u></a> By default, Samsung Internet Browser enables the “Smart anti-tracking“ function that will help block third parties attempting to track your personal information.</p><p style="margin-left:1em;"><a href="https://support.brave.com/hc/en-us/articles/360050634931"><u>Brave:</u></a> By default, Brave protects you from cross-site tracking by blocking third-party cookies.</p><p>For more information about other browsers, please refer to this <a href="https://www.allaboutcookies.org/manage-cookies/">“All About Cookies” guide</a>. For more information about trackers, including information about how to manage and delete trackers, please visit the <a href="https://ico.org.uk/for-the-public/online/cookies/">ICO’s website</a>.</p><p>To opt out of Google Analytics data collection, follow <a href="https://tools.google.com/dlpage/gaoptout">these Google instructions</a>.</p><p>To reset your device identifier, follow <a href="https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/6048248?hl=en">Google instructions</a> and <a href="https://support.apple.com/en-us/HT205223">Apple instructions</a>.</p><p>The third-party advertisers, ad agencies and other vendors with which we work may be members of the Network Advertising Initiative (NAI), the Digital Advertising Alliance (DAA) Self-Regulatory Program for Online Behavioural Advertising and/or the European Digital Advertising Alliance (eDAA). To opt out of interest-based advertising from the participating companies, please visit <a href="http://optout.aboutads.info/?c=2&lang=EN">AboutAds.info</a> or <a href="http://www.youronlinechoices.eu/">the European Digital Advertising Alliance</a> for laptops and <a href="https://www.networkadvertising.org/mobile-choice/">NAI Mobile Choices</a> or <a href="https://youradchoices.com/appchoices">AppChoices</a> for mobile devices. Note that opting out through these channels does not mean you will no longer see ads and is specific to the device and browser you are using. You will still receive other types of ads from these companies, and any type of ad from nonparticipating companies. The sites you visit may still collect your information for other purposes.</p><p>Your browser may offer you a "Do Not Track" option, which allows you to signal to operators of websites and web applications and services (including behavioral advertising services) that you do not wish such operators to track certain of your online activities over time and across different websites. Please note that The Athletic does not support Do Not Track requests at this time, which means that we collect information about your online activity while you are using The Athletic.</p><p><strong>Contact Us</strong></p><p>If you have any queries regarding this Cookie Policy, please contact us at privacy@nytimes.com. If you have any questions regarding The Athletic, please contact The Athletic at privacy@theathletic.com.</p></div>

https://help.nytimes.com/115002797688-Po.visible_text: The New York Times Company Cookie Policy - The New York Times Help Center Due to higher than normal volume, we anticipate long wait times. You can manage your account online at nytimes.com/account. HELP CENTER Your Account | NYTimes.com Help > Permissions and Policies > Policies The New York Times Company Cookie Policy Table of Contents 1. What Is a Tracker? 2. What Trackers Do We Use And For Which Purpose? 3. How Do I Manage Trackers? English (US) FR French BR Portuguese (Brazil) US English (US) CN Chinese MX Spanish (Mexico) Effective on September 9, 2024 This Cookie Policy explains how we use cookies and similar tracking methods (such as pixels, SDKs, JavaScript, local storage, device identifiers, etc., which we refer to as “trackers”) when you visit our site. “Our site” means our websites, emails, apps and other services that link to this Cookie Policy, like nytimes.com and its subdomains, including The Athletic and Wirecutter. This policy explains what various tracking methods are, and why they are used. It also explains your right to control their use. We may change this Cookie Policy at any time. Check the “last revised” date at the top of this page to see when this Cookie Policy was last revised. Any change becomes effective when we post the revised Cookie Policy on or through our site. Where we use trackers to collect information that is personally identifiable, or that can become personally identifiable if we combine it with other information, our Privacy Policy will apply in addition to this Cookie Policy. If you have any questions, please contact us by email at privacy@nytimes.com. You can also write to us: The New York Times Company, 620 Eighth Avenue, New York, N.Y. 10018, attn.: Legal Department. If you have any questions regarding The Athletic, please contact The Athletic at privacy@theathletic.com. Table of Conten 1. What Is a Tracker? We use a variety of tracker methods; six of the main types are explained below. This list is intended to include all categories that we use, although the categories may vary depending on the use of our site. We use trackers to enable our servers to recognize your web browser and tell us how and when you visit and otherwise use the services through the internet, to analyze trends, and to learn about our user base so that we can improve our services and your experience. We may combine non-personally identifiable information collected through trackers with other personal information that we have about you, for example, to tell us who you are or whether you have an account. We may also supplement the information we collect from you with information received from third parties in order to enhance our services, or to offer you information that we believe may be of interest to you. Please reference the descriptions below to learn more about the kinds of trackers we use and for what purpose. A) Cookies A cookie is a small string of text that a website (or online service) stores on a user’s browser. It saves data on your browser about your visit to our site or other sites. It often includes a unique identifier (e.g., cookie #123). “First-party cookies” are cookies set by us (or on our behalf) on our site. “Third-party cookies” are cookies set by other companies whose functionality is embedded into our site (e.g., google.com). “Session cookies” are temporary cookies stored on your device while you visit our site. They expire when you close your browser. “Persistent cookies” are stored on your browser for a period of time after you leave our site. Persistent cookies expire on a set expiration date, or when they are deleted manually. We use persistent cookies to store your preferences so that they are available for the next visit. This allows us, for example, to keep a more accurate account of how often you visit our services, how often you return, how your use of the services may vary over time, to target advertising, and measure the effectiveness of advertising efforts. Just like any other usage information we collect, this information allows us to improve the services and customize your online experience. You can choose whether to accept cookies by editing your browser settings. However, if cookies are refused, your experience on our site may be worse, and some features may not work as intended. B) Pixels Pixels (also known as “web beacons,” “GIFs” or “bugs”) are one-pixel transparent images located on web pages or messages. They track whether you have opened these web pages or messages. Upon firing, a pixel logs a visit to the current page or message and may read or set cookies. Pixels often rely on cookies to work, so turning off cookies can impair them. But even if you turn off cookies, pixels can still detect a web page visit. C) Javascript JavaScript is a programming language. It can be used to write trackers that, when embedded into a page, allow us to measure how you interact with our site and other sites. D) Software Development Kits (or SDKs) SDKs are pieces of code provided by our digital vendors (e.g., third-party advertising companies, ad networks and analytics providers) in our mobile apps to collect and analyze certain device and user data. E) Device Identifiers Device identifiers are user-resettable identifiers comprised of numbers and letters. They are unique to a specific device. They are stored directly on the device. They are used to recognize you and/or your devices(s) on, off and across different apps and devices for marketing and advertising purposes. F) ID Synching In order to decide what type of ad might interest you, our digital and marketing vendors sometimes link data — inferred from your browsing of other sites or collected from other sources — using a method knowns as “ID synching” or “cookie synching.” To do this, they match the tracker ID they have assigned to you with one or more tracker IDs that are held in another company’s database and that are likely also associated with you. Any of the linked trackers may have certain interests and other demographic information attributed to it. That information is then used to determine which ad to show you. 2. What Trackers Do We Use And For Which Purpose? Below is a list of the types of trackers that appear on our site. Essential Trackers Essential trackers are required for our site to operate and to provide you with the features or services that you have requested. They allow you to navigate our site and use its services and features (e.g., cookies that help you stay logged in). Without essential trackers, our site will not run smoothly; in fact, our site (or certain services or features) might not even be available to you simply because of technical limitations. Analytics Trackers Analytics trackers collect or use information about your site use, which helps us improve our site. Among the uses of analytics trackers are to show us which pages are most frequently visited, help us record difficulties you have with our site, track subscription purchases and behaviors leading to subscription purchases, and measure how well ads perform. These trackers add up our readers’ visits to show us larger patterns in our audience. We look at these larger patterns to analyze site traffic. Marketing Trackers These trackers help us determine which ads to show you for Times properties — both on our site and on other sites. To do this, these trackers use information about your behavior on various sites to target our ads. These trackers allow us to limit the number of times you see our ad across your devices. They help us personalize the ads we show you. They also enable us to measure the effectiveness of our marketing campaigns (e.g., measure if you subscribe after seeing our ads). Advertising Trackers Advertising trackers help us and our advertising partners to determine which ads from third parties are selected for you. Some of these trackers collect or use information about your behavior and browsing habits on our services and other sites (including the pages you have visited, and the links and advertisements you have clicked). They also collect your demographic details, interests and certain technical information about your browser or device to aid this targeting. These trackers sometimes limit the number of times you see an ad, make an ad more relevant to you or measure the effectiveness of an ad campaign. We may not have control or access to such trackers. If you look at one page on our services, an advertisement may be delivered to you on our services or on other sites, for products referenced on that page or for similar products and services. We work with advertisers, ad agencies and other vendors to serve these ads, who often use their own trackers through our site. The ads served can include additional trackers which are activated when an ad is visible to you or when you click on or otherwise interact with an ad. 3. How Do I Manage Trackers? In certain jurisdictions, when you first come to our site, you will receive a banner notification that trackers are present. By clicking or tapping “accept all,” you agree to the use of these trackers as described here. You can manage your tracker settings at any time by clicking on “Manage Privacy Preferences” in our website footer or in your app “Privacy Settings”, or “Account Settings” for the Athletic app. In addition, you can refuse or accept trackers from our site (or any other site) in your browser’s settings. If you refuse trackers, you might not be able to sign in or use other tracker-dependent features of our site. Most browsers automatically accept cookies, but this is typically something you can adjust. Information for each browser can be found in the links below: Safari on desktop and Safari Mobile (iPhone and iPads) : Note that, by default, Safari is engineered to protect you from being tracked from site to site unless you disable Intelligent Tracking Prevention (ITP). Firefox: By default, Firefox protects you from cross-site tracking so long as you have not disabled Total Cookie Protection. There is therefore less need to manage cookies to protect your privacy. Chrome Microsoft Edge: Enabling tracking prevention with Edge will protect you from being tracked between sites, such that there will be less of a need to manage your cookies in order to protect your privacy. Samsung Internet Browser: By default, Samsung Internet Browser enables the “Smart anti-tracking“ function that will help block third parties attempting to track your personal information. Brave: By default, Brave protects you from cross-site tracking by blocking third-party cookies. For more information about other browsers, please refer to this “All About Cookies” guide . For more information about trackers, including information about how to manage and delete trackers, please visit the ICO’s website . To opt out of Google Analytics data collection, follow these Google instructions . To reset your device identifier, follow Google instructions and Apple instructions . The third-party advertisers, ad agencies and other vendors with which we work may be members of the Network Advertising Initiative (NAI), the Digital Advertising Alliance (DAA) Self-Regulatory Program for Online Behavioural Advertising and/or the European Digital Advertising Alliance (eDAA). To opt out of interest-based advertising from the participating companies, please visit AboutAds.info or the European Digital Advertising Alliance for laptops and NAI Mobile Choices or AppChoices for mobile devices. Note that opting out through these channels does not mean you will no longer see ads and is specific to the device and browser you are using. You will still receive other types of ads from these companies, and any type of ad from nonparticipating companies. The sites you visit may still collect your information for other purposes. Your browser may offer you a "Do Not Track" option, which allows you to signal to operators of websites and web applications and services (including behavioral advertising services) that you do not wish such operators to track certain of your online activities over time and across different websites. Please note that The Athletic does not support Do Not Track requests at this time, which means that we collect information about your online activity while you are using The Athletic. Contact Us If you have any queries regarding this Cookie Policy, please contact us at privacy@nytimes.com. If you have any questions regarding The Athletic, please contact The Athletic at privacy@theathletic.com. Was this article helpful? Can't find what you're looking for?
